chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 41 to 50, the decade of sulking (புலவிப் பத்து) in Orampokiyar's marutham hundred: the wife and her friend refuse the husband who comes back from the courtesan, mocking his chest, his oaths and his bard, setting their pallor against his rich river town, and using the bard-women's barter of fish for grain and the tortoise and crocodile of the pond as images of his care and his cruelty.

41.reading: Speaking of the man in the third person, the woman says his town is said to have a pond of white flowers with a loveless crocodile that eats its own young, and that is why the lord of that town turns gold-pale the bodies of those who took his word as true.
41.nuance: The crocodile that devours its own young is the hidden image a reader expects in marutham, but here அதனால் (therefore) states the inference outright: the town breeds such a lord. So it fails ullurai condition 2 and stands as a juxtaposition; the plural உணர்ந்தோர் makes her one of several women he has paled.

thinai_evidence.note: a town-lord whose trusted word leaves women pale: the marutham wife's grievance

comparisons.tenor: the pallor of the trusting women's skin
the lord who ruins those who depend on his word

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the colophon has no thurai. He is spoken of as அவன், so the addressee is someone other than the man, most likely the friend.

42.reading: The friend asks the man of the rich town whether his well-jewelled wife has lost her wits from too much joy, that she has begun to thrust away his chest, broad as the full flood of the Kaviri.
42.nuance: The question is ironic: what the friend calls a joy-drunk delusion is the wife's deliberate sulk. The flood simile flatters his chest and at the same time marks it as something that sweeps over everything in its path.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's refusal of her husband's chest is oodal

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the colophon has no thurai. நின் மாண் இழை அரிவை names the wife to her husband, so the speaker is the friend.

43.reading: The woman tells the man of the rich town, where many copper-red young sleep on the back of a tortoise shaped like a measuring vessel, that his bard is an even greater liar than he is and swears many oaths.
43.nuance: நின்னினும் (more than you) is the sting: in calling the bard the greater liar she calls the husband a liar too. The young asleep on the tortoise's back might suggest the household resting on the man, but that is one match of mood, not two pairs, so it stays scene and simile.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard's false oaths on the husband's behalf belong to marutham sulking

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the colophon has no thurai. The speaker could also be the friend.

44.reading: The friend tells the man that as the young of the tortoise in the sweet wide pond grow by looking at their mother's face, so is his chest to his wife; knowing this, he should act on it, for that is also virtue.
44.nuance: The old belief that the tortoise feeds its young by its gaze makes the claim exact: she needs only his presence, not his provision. The last words turn a love complaint into a matter of அறன், duty as well as feeling.

thinai_evidence.note: counsel to a straying husband in the marutham household

comparisons.tenor: the wife who lives by looking to her husband's chest

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the colophon has no thurai. ஐய is the friend's address to the man.

45.reading: The woman tells her husband that his town is adorned by a river which in the cold season brings cool muddy water and in summer takes the colour of sapphire, while her eyes are adorned with pallor.
45.nuance: The one verb அணி serves both halves: the river's changing colours adorn his town in every season, her only ornament is the colour of grief. The river that changes with the seasons may also hint at a man who changes, but the poem leaves that unsaid.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's pallor set against the husband's flourishing town

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the colophon has no thurai. மகிழ்ந and என் கண்ணே fix the speaker and addressee.

46.reading: With bitter irony the woman tells the man that it is pleasant not only for him but for her too that he lives there, as the bright-browed woman who loves his chest wished, and shows no grace here.
46.nuance: ஈண்டு (here) and ஆண்டு (there) carry the whole poem: two houses, and he has chosen the other. The praise of the rival as நன்னுதல் is part of the mockery.

thinai_evidence.note: a husband living with another woman: marutham's situation

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the colophon has no thurai.

47.reading: The woman tells the man of the town where his wife fills, with big striped-stalk beans, the wide basket in which the sharp-toothed bard-woman poured sweet ketiru fish, that her well-jewelled companions know he tells many lies, just like his bard.
47.nuance: A near miss for ullurai: the bard-woman bringing her catch into the wife's house could stand for the bard's go-between work, but the poem names only one situation (lying) and the barter gives no second pair; record it as scene. The witnesses are the companions, so the lie is public.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's lies told in a marutham barter-town

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the colophon has no thurai. It may also be the friend, since the ஆயம் is the wife's band of companions.

48.reading: The woman tells the man of the town where his wife fills, with white paddy kept for years, the basket in which the young daughter of the net-skilled bard poured varaal fish, that she does not want him coming here, lord, with the marks he made there with his other woman.
48.nuance: The bard family that trades fish at the door is the same that carries the husband's messages to the courtesan, which is why the barter can carry the sense. யாண்டு in line 3 (years) and யாண்டு in line 5 (there) are a pun the poem builds on.

thinai_evidence.note: refusing a husband who comes from the courtesan: marutham

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the colophon has no thurai. வேண்டேம் பெரும is the wife refusing him.

ullurai.tenor: the husband who brings the other woman's marks into the wife's house and expects to be received

pairs.situation: what the bard's people bring is poured into the wife's own basket, as he brings the courtesan's marks into her house
the wife pays with the store of past years, as she is expected to repay his visit with the love of their long marriage

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife uses the barter at her own door, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

49.reading: The woman asks the man of the rich town, where the soft-haired bard-woman of swaying gait pours out a few fish and gets much paddy, whose beauty his bard will now ruin with his lies.
49.nuance: Near miss for ullurai: few fish for much paddy matches the bard who gets much for a few false words, but the poem gives only that one correspondence (condition 3). இனியே (now) implies her own beauty is already spent: he has no one left to deceive here.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard's lies spoil a wife's beauty: marutham sulking

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the colophon has no thurai.

50.reading: The friend tells the man of the rich town where the vanji tree stands tall that the wealth of his household and they themselves suffer, that he gives no refuge, and that this woman who won his heart weeps as well.
50.nuance: Line 1 is hard: துணையோர் செல்வமும் may be the wealth of those bound to him, or the kin and their wealth together; either way the suffering is the household's, not the wife's alone, and இவளும் comes last as the climax.

thinai_evidence.note: a household left without the husband's grace: marutham

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: inferred; the colophon has no thurai. இவள் points to the wife beside the speaker, so the friend speaks.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 41 says the lord turns gold-pale the bodies of those who trusted his word; Akananuru 146 has the wife foresee that the next woman who believes the deceiver's word (வாய்மொழி நம்பி) will weep and go pale as she did.
links.teaches: Held together, the two show that pallor from a trusted word was a fixed charge against the marutham husband: the Ainkurunuru states it as a habit of his town in four lines, and the Akananuru turns the same charge into a forecast for the rival, so the wronged wife becomes the proof of what awaits the other woman.

links.note: In both the wife refuses the straying husband's chest: in Ainkurunuru 42 the friend reports it to him as if it were joy-drunk folly; in Kural 1311 the wife herself refuses it because all women feast on it with their eyes.
links.teaches: The refusal of the chest was a recognised act of the sulking wife before Valluvar; the Sangam friend presents it with mock surprise to shame the man, while the Kural gives the wife her own reason, so the couplet supplies the motive that the older poem leaves to irony.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 43 calls the husband's bard a bigger liar than the husband, full of oaths; Akananuru 56 shows that bard on the street hurrying to bring new brides to the lord, scared into the wife's own house by a cow, and laughed at.
links.teaches: The two give the bard's double role in marutham: the Ainkurunuru names the charge (he lies and swears for his master) and the Akananuru shows why the wife can mock him openly, since attacking the go-between lets her shame the husband without naming him.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 44 says the tortoise's young grow by looking at the mother's face; Siddhar 176 says the sea tortoise's eggs take form as the mother thinks of them, and asks when the poet will so reach God.
links.teaches: The same belief, that the tortoise nurtures without touch, serves the Sangam friend to argue that a wife needs only her husband's presence and the later siddhar to describe grace given by attention alone, so a piece of animal lore carried a model of care at a distance from household love into devotion.

links.note: In Ainkurunuru 49 the bard-woman pours a few fish and gets much paddy; in Akananuru 126 the bard's daughter in Evvi's Kaviri land will not even take old red paddy for her brothers' vaalai fish and is given pearls.
links.teaches: The barter of the bard's women was a stock picture of the bard family getting more than it gives; the Akananuru uses it as praise of a patron's wealth, while the Ainkurunuru turns the same profit into an accusation, since the bard who gets much for little also gets much for his lies.

links.note: Kural 1303 says that not embracing the one who sulks is like adding pain to those already in distress; Ainkurunuru 50 tells the husband who gives no refuge that the household and they suffer, and his wife weeps too.
links.teaches: The Kural states the cost of withheld grace for one sulking woman, while the Ainkurunuru friend counts it across the whole household, its wealth and its people, so the older poem makes the husband's refusal a failure of the house and not only of love.
